report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is **not established**. A vegetarian diet may improve some health-risk factors and may be associated with lower mortality in certain populations, but current observational evidence does not consistently show that vegetarians live longer than comparable meat eaters.

The strongest supportive result comes from Adventist Health Study-2: vegetarian dietary patterns were associated with lower all-cause mortality after adjustment for measured lifestyle and demographic factors. But this is an observational cohort, so differences such as health behaviors, socioeconomic factors, and diet quality may partly explain the association.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23836264/

In contrast, the EPIC-Oxford British cohort found no statistically significant difference in all-cause mortality between vegetarians and meat eaters.  
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0002916523238332

An umbrella review likewise reports that a meta-analysis of seven cohort studies found no significant reduction in all-cause mortality for vegetarian diets.  
https://hal.science/hal-03492615v1/document

Thus, replacing high amounts of red/processed meat with nutritious plant foods is plausibly beneficial, but simply adopting the vegetarian label does not reliably predict longer life. Overall dietary quality, smoking, alcohol use, physical activity, body weight, and access to healthcare are major determinants of life expectancy.
